section.title: The Devastation of the Earth
section.sectionRationale: This chapter opens what scholars often call the Isaiah apocalypse, chapters 24 to 27, where the prophet's gaze widens beyond any single nation to the whole earth and beyond any single historical crisis toward God's final judgment. The oracles against individual nations, chapters 13 to 23, now give way to a vision of universal devastation, universal guilt, and the LORD reigning gloriously on Mount Zion.
section.thesis: The LORD lays waste the whole earth because its people have broken the everlasting covenant, yet even amid this universal devastation scattered voices break out in praise, glory to the Righteous One, anticipating the day the LORD reigns openly on Mount Zion before His elders.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the LORD twisting and emptying the earth; the earth mourning under a curse for breaking the everlasting covenant; the city of chaos shattered and joy exiled; scattered voices of praise amid terror, glory to the Righteous One; and the earth split open as the LORD comes to reign on Zion.

units.label: The LORD lays waste the earth

verses.text: Behold, the LORD lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins. He will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants,
people and priest alike, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor.
The earth will be utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered. For the LORD has spoken this word.

units.label: Mourning under a curse for a broken covenant

verses.text: The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades; the exalted of the earth waste away.
The earth is defiled by its people; they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the {{beritOlam|everlasting covenant}}.
Therefore a curse has consumed the earth, and its inhabitants must bear the guilt; the earth's dwellers have been burned, and only a few survive.
The new wine dries up, the vine withers. All the merrymakers now groan.
The joyful tambourines have ceased; the noise of revelers has stopped; the joyful harp is silent.
They no longer sing and drink wine; strong drink is bitter to those who consume it.
The city of chaos is shattered; every house is closed to entry.
In the streets they cry out for wine. All joy turns to gloom; rejoicing is exiled from the land.
The city is left in ruins; its gate is reduced to rubble.
So will it be on the earth and among the nations, like a harvested olive tree, like a gleaning after a grape harvest.

units.label: Voices of praise amid the terror

verses.text: They raise their voices, they shout for joy; from the west they proclaim the majesty of the LORD.
Therefore glorify the LORD in the east. Extol the name of the LORD, the God of Israel in the islands of the sea.
From the ends of the earth we hear singing: “Glory to the Righteous One.” But I said, “I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me.” The treacherous betray; the treacherous deal in treachery.
Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of the earth.
Whoever flees the sound of panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are open, and the foundations of the earth are shaken.

units.label: The earth split open, the LORD reigns on Zion

verses.text: The earth is utterly broken apart, the earth is split open, the earth is shaken violently.
The earth staggers like a drunkard and sways like a shack. Earth's rebellion weighs it down, and it falls, never to rise again.
In that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below.
They will be gathered together like prisoners in a pit. They will be confined to a dungeon and punished after many days.
The moon will be confounded and the sun will be ashamed; for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders with great glory.

beritOlam.gloss: An everlasting covenant, a phrase used elsewhere for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, and David. Its breaking here by the earth's whole population, not Israel alone, suggests a violation of the moral order woven into creation itself, the reason the whole earth, not one nation, now lies under judgment.

basic.context: Isaiah's gaze suddenly widens from individual nations to the entire earth. Every class of person, priest and people, master and servant, buyer and seller, is swept into the same devastation, because the earth's inhabitants have broken an everlasting covenant. Yet even in this bleak vision, scattered voices break out from every direction singing glory to the Righteous One, and the chapter ends with the LORD reigning gloriously on Mount Zion.
basic.hermeneutics: Chapters 24 to 27 are often called the Isaiah apocalypse because their scope moves beyond any single historical judgment toward a more universal, cosmic horizon, though scholars debate exactly how much this looks to near history and how much to the final end. This chapter's vision of a completely leveled city and a whole earth judged for breaking a covenant likely draws together both, a near historical judgment on human pride and a genuine foretaste of the final judgment and reign of God, and readers should hold its details with real interpretive humility rather than forcing a single timetable onto it.
basic.originalLanguages: The word eretz, earth or land, recurs so often that it becomes almost a drumbeat through the chapter, insisting this judgment is not local but total. At its center stands the charge that humanity broke the berit olam, the everlasting covenant, language elsewhere reserved for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, and David, suggesting a violation of creation's basic moral order.
basic.typology: The LORD reigning openly on Mount Zion before His elders with great glory, verse 23, anticipates the full, visible reign of Christ, who will judge and reign over all the earth. The everlasting covenant broken by humanity here anticipates the new and better everlasting covenant God establishes through Christ's blood, Hebrews 13:20.
basic.christ: The chapter's closing vision of the LORD reigning gloriously on Mount Zion before His elders anticipates Christ's coming kingdom, when He who judges the earth in righteousness will reign visibly and forever, Revelation 11:15. Where humanity broke the everlasting covenant and brought the earth's curse, Christ establishes an everlasting covenant that cannot be broken, sealed in His own blood, Hebrews 13:20.
basic.god: God's judgment here reaches everyone, without regard to social status, because the underlying offense, breaking His everlasting covenant, belongs to humanity as a whole, not one class or nation. Yet even in this sweeping judgment He is not silent toward praise; voices rise from every direction glorifying Him as the Righteous One, and His reign on Zion is the chapter's final, glorious word.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 9:16 and Genesis 17:7 establish earlier everlasting covenants that this chapter's broken covenant echoes and intensifies. Romans 8:19-22 describes creation groaning under the weight of human sin, awaiting redemption, much like this chapter's mourning earth. Hebrews 13:20 names the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood as eternal. Revelation 11:15 announces the final reign of Christ, echoing this chapter's vision of the LORD reigning on Zion.
basic.oneStory: This chapter widens Isaiah's vision from individual nations to the whole earth, judged for breaking God's everlasting covenant, yet ends in praise and the LORD's glorious reign on Zion. It is a foretaste of the final judgment and kingdom of Christ, who both judges the earth's rebellion and establishes an everlasting covenant that will never be broken.

context.literary:
Every earlier oracle in this part of Isaiah carries a heading and a target, 'the burden against' Babylon, Moab, Egypt or Tyre. Isaiah 24 has neither. No nation is named, no city is named, and the grammatical subject of nearly every clause is the earth. The BSB uses the word seventeen times in twenty-three verses, and verse 4 doubles it with a second word for the inhabited world. The reader has been walked through the neighbors one by one, and now the camera pulls back to take in everything at once.

The chapter moves in four waves. Verses 1 to 3 announce a total emptying, with verb forms that double for emphasis, 'utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered.' Verse 2 gives a list of six matched pairs, people and priest, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor, each introduced by the same comparison, so that whatever happens to one happens to the other. No social position gives cover. Verses 4 to 13 set out the mourning of the earth, the reason for it in verses 5 and 6, the silence of the feasts in verses 7 to 9, and the ruined city in verses 10 to 12, and they end with a harvest image, a beaten olive tree and the leftovers of a vintage, verse 13. Verses 14 to 16a are a startling burst of song, from the west, the east, the coastlands and the ends of the earth. Verses 16b to 22 return to the pit and the snare and the collapsing earth, and then widen upward to the host of heaven.

The whole chapter turns on one first-person line, 'But I said, "I am wasting away!"' verse 16, where the prophet interrupts the choir with his own terror. It is the one place where a human voice speaks for itself in a chapter of divine action. Its beginning and its end are held together by the LORD, who 'lays waste the earth' in verse 1 and 'will reign on Mount Zion' in verse 23. The only phrase that marks time is 'in that day,' verse 21, a refrain that governs chapters 25 to 27.

The gaze also climbs. Verses 1 to 17 stay on earth, and from verse 18 the windows of heaven open, verse 21 turns to the host of heaven above, and verse 23 ends with the moon and sun shamed.
context.historical:
Isaiah's world was one of repeated catastrophe. Assyria had taken Samaria and carried its people away, 2 Kings 17:6, and in 701 BC took every fortified city of Judah, Isaiah 36:1. People who heard these words could look at a landscape in which vineyards had been cut down, feasts had ceased and cities stood open. The chapter draws on that experience, and its ordinary images, the new wine, the vine, the tambourine and the harp, are the instruments of ancient joy, as Isaiah 5:12 shows when it lists the lyre, harp, tambourine, flute and wine at the feasts of the heedless. Jeremiah later announces the banishment of 'the sounds of joy and gladness,' Jeremiah 25:10, in the same terms.

The Hebrew word eretz means both 'land' and 'earth,' and the chapter profits from the ambiguity. The first hearers could take it as the land of Judah, ruined as Samaria had been, and then hear it widen to the whole world. Scholars who read the chapter as part of the original Isaiah place it in the eighth century. Many others date chapters 24 to 27, which are often called the Isaiah apocalypse, to later centuries, after the fall of Jerusalem. Either way, the reader meets a collection of oracles gathered after the oracles against the nations, and the chapter functions as their summary.

The covenant background is also old. Israel's treaty tradition invoked heaven and earth as witnesses to the covenant, Deuteronomy 30:19 and Isaiah 1:2, so that if the covenant were broken, creation itself was a party to the lawsuit. The curses listed in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 include barren land, siege and exile, all of which appear in this chapter in condensed form. The 'city of chaos' is not identified. Some propose Babylon, some propose Jerusalem, and later in the same section a lofty city is humbled in 26:5 and a fortified town is left a ruin in 25:2.
context.canonical:
Chapter 24 opens a sequence that does not end until chapter 27. The next chapter turns the same mountain, Zion, into the place of a feast for all peoples, where the LORD 'will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:6-8, a line that Paul cites to describe the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:54. Isaiah 26:19 promises that the dead will live, and Isaiah 27:1 promises that the LORD will slay the dragon of the sea. The devastation of chapter 24 is the first movement of a larger piece in which the earth is judged, then healed.

The chapter picks up Genesis. The 'windows of heaven' open in verse 18 as the floodgates opened in Noah's day, Genesis 7:11, the covenant broken is called everlasting as the covenant after the flood was, Genesis 9:16, and the 'curse' that devours the earth in verse 6 recalls the cursed ground of Genesis 3:17. The dissolving of creation resembles Jeremiah's vision, in which the earth is again formless and void, Jeremiah 4:23-28, and Hosea's mourning land, Hosea 4:1-3. Zephaniah 1:2-3 and Isaiah 13:10-13 make similar announcements of a world swept bare and a sky darkened.

The New Testament reads the chapter's end as a picture of the last day. The sun darkened and the stars falling, Revelation 6:12-14 and Matthew 24:29, the great earthquake, Revelation 16:18-20, and the world's elements dissolving, 2 Peter 3:10-13, take the same shape. Hebrews adds that God will shake not only the earth but heaven, so that 'the unshakable may remain,' Hebrews 12:26-27. The imprisonment of verse 22 finds a parallel in the binding of the dragon in Revelation 20:1-3, and the reign on Zion corresponds to Revelation 11:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wants his hearers to see that the judgments they have been hearing, on Babylon, Moab, Egypt and Tyre, are not separate dramas. They are installments of a single verdict. The earth is guilty, and the nations are the places where that guilt becomes visible. For people who had been watching their neighbors fall and quietly thinking they were exempt, this is a chapter that closes the exits.

But the prophet also wants them to know why. The reason is not capricious, and it is not bad luck. Verse 5 says the people have violated laws, decrees and an everlasting covenant, and verse 6 says the curse is the result. Isaiah teaches that moral order is built into the world and that rebellion is not free. He places a counterweight in the middle of the wreck, the song of verses 14 to 16, so that hearers are not left with despair. People will praise the LORD from the farthest places even as the old order cracks, and in the end it is the LORD, not the earth's lords, who reigns, verse 23. The intended response is sober repentance and a hope that does not rest on anything in the world that can be shaken.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God will do and why, and it does not give a program for any individual. Verse 2 lists social pairs to say that no class escapes. It is not a list of vocations to avoid, and no one should read 'buyer and seller' or 'priest' as a condemnation of ordinary work or ministry. The prophet's cry in verse 16, 'I am wasting away,' is a record of how a faithful man felt, not an instruction to despair.

The apocalyptic images, the earth staggering like a drunkard, the host of heaven imprisoned, the moon confounded, are poetry on a cosmic scale, and the New Testament shows how to carry them. Peter does not use the day of the Lord to speculate but to ask what kind of people believers ought to be, 'in holiness and godliness,' 2 Peter 3:11. Hebrews does not use the shaking to stir fear but gratitude, 'since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom,' Hebrews 12:28. The chapter is meant to produce a life that holds this world loosely and worships freely, not a calendar of the end.

debates.question: Which covenant has the earth's inhabitants broken in verse 5?

views.label: The covenant with Noah
views.case: The only other place in Scripture where an 'everlasting covenant' is said to be made with the whole earth is Genesis 9:16, with 'every living creature of every kind that is on the earth.' The chapter's language is universal, the windows of heaven open in verse 18 as in the flood, Genesis 7:11, and Genesis 9 deals with bloodshed, which in Numbers 35:33 pollutes the land. This is the best fit for a charge laid against the whole world.

views.label: The Sinai covenant, broken by Israel
views.case: Verse 5 says the people 'transgressed the laws' and 'overstepped the decrees,' which is the language of the Torah, and verse 6 speaks of a curse, as in Leviticus 26:14-15 and Deuteronomy 28:15. Daniel 9:11 says that 'the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses' were poured out. On this reading, the chapter begins with Judah's ruin, which then becomes a pattern for the world.

views.label: A creation covenant, or the moral order written on every human being
views.case: Hosea 6:7 says that 'like Adam' they transgressed the covenant, and Paul says that the whole world is accountable to God, Romans 3:19, and that God's wrath is revealed against all human wickedness, Romans 1:18. On this view the 'everlasting covenant' names the standing obligation of every creature to the Creator.

debates.bearing: These readings are not exclusive. The Noah covenant explains why the whole earth is addressed, the language of laws and decrees reflects the Torah, and the creation order underlies both. The chapter charges humanity with covenant-breaking and leaves the precise covenant partly open.

debates.question: Is the chapter about a historical judgment, or the end of history?

views.label: A judgment within history, expressed in cosmic language
views.case: Prophets regularly describe the fall of a city or nation as the shaking of the heavens. Isaiah 13:10 uses sun, moon and stars to describe Babylon's fall, and verse 19 of this chapter can read as the same kind of poetry. The 'city of chaos' would be a particular city.

views.label: A vision of the last day
views.case: The scale, no nation named, the earth falling 'never to rise again,' verse 20, the host of heaven punished and the reign of the LORD on Zion with the sun and moon shamed, goes beyond any recorded event. The New Testament reads the images that way, Revelation 6:12-14 and 2 Peter 3:10-13.

views.label: A pattern in which the nearer events foretell the final one
views.case: Isaiah sees each historical devastation as a preview. The Assyrian ruin of Judah's land and the later fall of Jerusalem are real and are meant as warnings, and they are also forerunners of the ultimate day.

debates.bearing: The third reading does the most justice to the text, whose language of ruin is concrete enough to warn Judah and wide enough to reach the last day. Readers are wise to hold the timetable loosely.

debates.question: Who are 'the host of heaven above' in verse 21?

views.label: Spiritual powers behind the nations
views.case: The verse sets 'the host of heaven above' beside 'the kings of the earth below,' a pairing of heavenly and earthly rulers. Scripture elsewhere hints that spiritual powers stand behind the nations, Deuteronomy 32:8, Psalm 82:1 and 82:7, Daniel 10:13, and Paul speaks of 'spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 6:12. The imprisonment in a pit then matches the chaining of the powers of evil, 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6.

views.label: The stars and the gods the nations worshiped
views.case: The 'host of heaven' is a regular phrase for sun, moon and stars, which Deuteronomy 4:19 warns Israel not to worship. The moon and sun are 'confounded' and 'ashamed' in verse 23, language fitted to rival objects of worship, and the verse may be saying that the gods of the nations are exposed as nothing.

views.label: A poetic way of saying that the highest powers are brought low
views.case: Some take the pair as a general picture of every exalted power, heavenly and earthly, being subject to the LORD. This fits Isaiah's habit of describing the humbling of those who think themselves high, Isaiah 2:12 and 26:5.

debates.bearing: The first two readings are close, because the nations' gods and the powers behind them are tied together in Scripture. What matters for the chapter is that no height, earthly or heavenly, is out of the LORD's reach.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening verbs of the chapter rhyme. In verse 1 the LORD 'lays waste' the earth and 'leaves it in ruins,' two participles whose sounds, in Hebrew, echo each other, as though the language itself had been emptied out. Verse 3 doubles the verbs with the Hebrew device of an infinitive before a finite form, which the BSB renders as 'utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered.' The device is the same one that gave 'you will surely die' in Genesis 2:17. The overwhelming force of the chapter's language is part of its meaning.

In verse 5 the earth is 'defiled' by its people. The verb means to be polluted or profaned, and it is the verb of Numbers 35:33, 'Do not pollute the land where you live, for bloodshed pollutes the land.' Psalm 106:38 uses it of the land polluted with innocent blood. The charge, then, is not only that laws were broken but that the ground has been stained. The verb that the BSB renders as 'broken' in the phrase 'broken the everlasting covenant' is the usual one for annulling a covenant, as in Leviticus 26:15.

In verse 6 the 'curse' is a word that also means an oath. It is the 'oath and the curse' of Daniel 9:11, the sanction attached to a sworn covenant. The people 'must bear the guilt,' a verb from the root behind the Hebrew word for a guilt offering. The language is that of a courtroom and a sanctuary together: the oath is enforced, and the guilt is real.

The 'city of chaos,' verse 10, uses the word tohu, 'formless,' the very word of Genesis 1:2, and the word Jeremiah uses when he sees the earth 'formless and void,' Jeremiah 4:23. Isaiah 45:18 says God 'did not create it to be empty,' using the same word. The city is the world's order reversed, a creation returned to its first emptiness.

In verse 17 the three words for terror, pit and snare are pachad, pachat and pach, a rhyming triplet that is easy to hear and hard to escape. Jeremiah 48:43-44 gives the same triplet against Moab. Isaiah has made a proverb out of it, the verbs of verse 16 pile up on the same idea, and the word for treachery, bagad, is repeated four times in a single sentence.

In verse 16 the cry is 'Glory to the Righteous One.' The Hebrew word for glory here is tsevi, which also means beauty, the word used in Isaiah 23:9 for the glory the LORD planned to disgrace in Tyre. The beauty that was stripped from the proud is given, by the singers, to the Righteous One.

Finally, in verse 18 the windows of heaven are opened. The noun for windows and the verb for opened are the same as in the account of Noah's flood, though the BSB renders Genesis 7:11 as 'floodgates.' And in verses 21 and 22 the verb to punish is a root that also means to visit or to attend to, so the sentence 'will be punished after many days' can be read as a visit that comes at the proper time.

typology.type: The windows of heaven and the days of Noah, Isaiah 24:18
typology.fulfillment: The waters of Noah's flood were the judgment that the earth's violence called down, and the ark carried eight people through it, 1 Peter 3:20. Isaiah 24 uses the same language of opened windows and shaken foundations, and Jesus says that the coming of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah, with people eating and drinking until the flood came, Matthew 24:37-39. Peter makes the pattern explicit: the world of that time perished by water, and the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, 2 Peter 3:5-7. The escalation is that the ark becomes Christ, in whom the person is carried through judgment by the resurrection, 1 Peter 3:21. The type is partial, since the flood ended with a promise never to repeat it, Genesis 9:11, and the final judgment does not.

typology.type: The host of heaven shut up in a pit, Isaiah 24:21-22
typology.fulfillment: The powers above and the kings below are gathered like prisoners and confined to a dungeon. At the cross Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them, Colossians 2:15, and God seated Him 'far above all rule and authority, power and dominion,' Ephesians 1:20-22. The final stage is Revelation 20:1-3, where the dragon is seized, chained, thrown into the Abyss and sealed in. The correspondence is of defeated powers held in prison until their final judgment. The type unfolds in stages, so that Isaiah's single scene is spread across the cross, the present reign and the end.

typology.type: Sun and moon shamed before a greater light, Isaiah 24:23
typology.fulfillment: The lights of heaven are put to shame because the LORD reigns in a glory that surpasses them. At Calvary the sun was darkened, Luke 23:44-45, as the Son of Man suffered, and Jesus promised that after the tribulation the sun would be darkened and the Son of Man would appear in the clouds with power and great glory, Matthew 24:29-30. The end of the story is a city with no need of sun or moon, 'because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23, as Isaiah 60:19-20 had promised. The darkness at the cross is an echo and not a declared fulfilment, but the final scene fills in what the shaming of the sun and moon pointed to.

typology.type: The elders before the glory of the LORD, Isaiah 24:23
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai the elders of Israel went up with Moses, saw the God of Israel and ate and drank without harm, Exodus 24:9-11. Isaiah's elders stand in the presence of the LORD's reign on Zion, and the next chapter spreads a feast for all peoples on the same mountain, Isaiah 25:6. Jesus gives His disciples a kingdom so that they may 'eat and drink at My table in My kingdom,' Luke 22:29-30, and Revelation speaks of the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The escalation is that the feast is not for seventy elders but for 'a kingdom and priests' drawn from every tribe, Revelation 5:9-10.

typology.type: The gleaned olive tree and the few who remain, Isaiah 24:6 and 24:13
typology.fulfillment: The survivors are described as the gleanings after the harvest, a remnant that Isaiah sees throughout the book, Isaiah 1:9 and 10:22. Paul takes up the same shape and says 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5, and he pictures the people of God as an olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted, Romans 11:17. In Christ the remnant is gathered, and in Him the outsiders from the coastlands join it. The type is imperfect, since Isaiah's olive tree is beaten by judgment, while Paul's is nourished by a root.

study.christ:
The chapter reaches Christ first through the figure it names in verse 16, the Righteous One. The Hebrew can be taken as God or as the righteous people in whom God is glorified, and the New Testament identifies the Righteous One in the flesh. Peter says to the crowd, 'You rejected the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, and Peter's letter says that 'Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18. Isaiah himself would later call the Servant 'My righteous Servant,' who will 'justify many,' Isaiah 53:11. The song that erupts from the earth's far edges in the middle of a chapter of ruin finds its true object in Him.

The second link is the song's geography. 'From the west,' 'in the east,' 'in the islands of the sea' and 'from the ends of the earth,' verses 14 to 16, describe praise coming from every direction, from the very coasts that Isaiah's contemporaries thought of as remote. The servant who is a light to the nations and a bringer of salvation 'to the ends of the earth,' Isaiah 49:6, is the figure whom the apostles say they proclaim, Acts 13:47. Paul gathers Isaiah's hope into a chain of texts about the Gentiles praising the Lord and ends with 'in Him the Gentiles will put their hope,' Romans 15:9-12. The islands that sing in Isaiah 24 are the first fruits of a mission that Christ commissions.

The third link is the covenant. The earth has broken an everlasting covenant and a curse consumes it, verses 5 and 6. Jesus says at the Last Supper, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28, and Hebrews speaks of 'the blood of the eternal covenant,' Hebrews 13:20. Paul says Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The curse of Isaiah 24:6 meets the Man who takes it upon Himself.

The fourth link is the final reign. The shaming of the host of heaven and the sun and moon, and the LORD's reign with His elders, are fulfilled in the One who has been raised 'far above all rule and authority,' Ephesians 1:20-22, who will hand the kingdom to the Father after destroying every enemy, the last of which is death, 1 Corinthians 15:24-26, and about whom the loud voices say 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15.

Care is needed. The chapter does not mention a Messiah, and its imagery should not be forced into a code. The links above depend on what the New Testament itself says about the Righteous One, the nations' praise, the covenant and the reign.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He is the subject at both ends of it. 'The LORD lays waste the earth,' verse 1, and 'the LORD of Hosts will reign,' verse 23. Between the two, the grammar of the verses slips into the passive, the earth mourns, the city is shattered, the gate is reduced to rubble, as though the damage has a momentum of its own. The frame says otherwise. The wreck is not an accident or an impersonal collapse. It is the act of a King who has spoken, 'For the LORD has spoken this word,' verse 3.

He is also a God of moral order. The chapter does not say that He is angry for no reason. It says that the earth is 'defiled by its people,' that they 'have transgressed the laws' and broken the covenant, and that therefore the curse has consumed it, verses 5 and 6. The judgment is the covenant's own sanction, as it was in Leviticus 26. A God who is faithful to His word must be faithful to His warnings. The earth is not a neutral stage on which He occasionally intervenes. It is His, and it bears the marks of the moral world He made.

He is impartial. The six pairs of verse 2 leave no one out, and the point is that priest and servant, creditor and debtor all stand alike before Him. The same impartiality is a mercy as well as a threat, for it means that no one is beyond His reach when He saves, either.

He is worthy of praise even in judgment. The chapter does not wait for the end of the storm to let the singing begin. 'From the ends of the earth we hear singing,' verse 16, and the singers sing of glory to the Righteous One. The people who hold on to Him are not the ones who have avoided the damage but those who recognize who is at work in it. The prophet himself is in anguish in the same verse, and the text allows both: real grief and real praise. A faithful response to God's judgments is not tidy.

He is also a patient and purposeful God. The imprisoned powers are punished 'after many days,' verse 22, which means that judgment is not an outburst but a considered act in due time. The King who reigns in verse 23 reigns on Mount Zion before His elders, a place of covenant, feast and presence, and this chapter opens onto the feast of Isaiah 25:6-8. For worship, the chapter teaches us to praise the LORD from wherever we are, to fear the God who keeps His word, and to hold what can be shaken loosely, since 'the unshakable' will remain, Hebrews 12:27.

crossReferences.note: The 'everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth' is the first covenant of that name. Isaiah 24:5 charges the earth's people with breaking a covenant of the same name and reach, so the Noahic covenant is the leading candidate for what is meant.

On the day the flood began, the fountains of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. Isaiah 24:18 uses the same words for the opening of heaven and the shaking of the earth's foundations, reading the coming judgment as a reversal of creation's stability.

Bloodshed pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for it except by the blood of the one who shed it. The verb for pollution is the one in Isaiah 24:5, and the verse explains how a violated moral order can leave the earth itself defiled.

The covenant's warnings begin with the people rejecting the statutes and breaking the covenant. Isaiah 24:5-6 reads like a sequel, with the same verb for breaking, and a curse that falls on land and people.

Jeremiah looks at the earth and finds it formless and void, the mountains quaking, the birds gone and the cities torn down. It is a creation in reverse, and it matches the 'city of chaos' of Isaiah 24:10 and the staggering earth of verse 20.

'Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab.' It is word for word the sequence of Isaiah 24:17-18, applied to a single nation. Isaiah takes a familiar proverb of doom and says it now applies to every dweller of the earth.

On this mountain the LORD of Hosts prepares a banquet for all peoples and swallows up death forever. It is the immediate sequel to the reign on Zion in Isaiah 24:23, and shows that the devastation of chapter 24 is the first act of a longer story that ends in a feast.

The elders of Israel saw the God of Israel and ate and drank in His presence. Isaiah's reference to the LORD reigning 'before His elders' in 24:23 hears an echo of Sinai, and the feast of chapter 25 completes the picture.

God promised to shake not only the earth but heaven, so that 'the unshakable may remain.' It reads Isaiah 24:18-20 as the removal of what can be shaken, and then draws the conclusion that believers receive a kingdom that cannot be.

The heavens will disappear with a roar and the earth will be laid bare, and believers look forward to 'a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.' It takes the cosmic language of Isaiah 24 and gives it a moral application and a hopeful end.

An angel seizes the dragon, binds him, throws him into the Abyss and seals it. The imprisonment in a pit of Isaiah 24:22, with punishment 'after many days,' finds a close narrative parallel in the binding of the dragon and his later release and final judgment.

The creation was subjected to futility in hope, and it groans as in the pains of childbirth. Where Isaiah 24:4 describes the earth mourning and withering under the curse, Paul explains the hope that the same creation will be set free.

Loud voices in heaven say that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ. It is the New Testament's version of the LORD reigning on Zion with great glory in Isaiah 24:23.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that Genesis 1 and 2 raise and Genesis 3 begins to answer, what happens to a world made for God's presence when its people break faith? Genesis 3:17 curses the ground because of Adam. Genesis 6 sees the earth filled with violence, and Genesis 7:11 opens the windows of heaven. After the flood, God establishes an everlasting covenant with every living creature, Genesis 9:16. Isaiah 24 is what it looks like when that covenant has been broken again, and the curse is not an individual's but a world's. The chapter takes the story of the first sin and the first flood and rewrites it with the whole of human history in view.

The chapter also fits the longer arc of Israel's story. Through the prophets, Israel's own breach of the covenant brings the curses of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, the land mourns, and the people are scattered, Hosea 4:1-3 and 2 Kings 17:6. Isaiah draws the lesson that Israel is not an exception but a sample. The whole world has broken faith, and Israel's exile is a preview of what its guilt deserves.

But the story does not end in ruin. Verses 14 to 16 give the first glimpse of the redeemed nations, singing from the corners of the earth. Chapters 25 to 27 follow, with the feast, the swallowing up of death, the dead rising and the dragon slain, Isaiah 25:6-8, 26:19, 27:1. The remnant is the seed from which the new people grow, and Jesus is the Righteous One who is the center of that people. His blood is the blood of the eternal covenant, Hebrews 13:20, and through Him the curse that consumed the earth is borne and lifted, Galatians 3:13.

The story ends with the shaking that leaves the unshakable. Peter looks for 'a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13, and Isaiah himself promises 'new heavens and a new earth,' Isaiah 65:17. In that world the 'city of chaos,' which was the world's own failed attempt at order, gives way to the city with strong walls and open gates, where a righteous nation enters, Isaiah 26:1-2. Revelation sees it come down, and God Himself dwelling with His people, Revelation 21:1-4. The curse of Isaiah 24 is the last curse, and the song of Isaiah 24:16 becomes the song of the whole earth.

quiz.q: Who is affected by the devastation described in verses 1 to 3?

options.text: Every class of person, without exception, priest and people, master and servant alike.
options.note: Verse 2 deliberately lists paired social classes to show total, impartial devastation.

options.text: Only the wealthy ruling classes.
options.note: The opposite; the text emphasizes that no class is exempt, not the wealthy alone.

options.text: Only foreign nations, not Israel or Judah.
options.note: The chapter's scope is the whole earth, not a foreign-nations-only judgment as in prior chapters.

options.text: Only those who worship idols.
options.note: Idolatry is part of the broader guilt named later, but verse 2 specifically stresses universal social scope, not a single sin category.

quiz.q: What underlying offense does verse 5 identify as the reason for this devastation?

options.text: Humanity has broken the everlasting covenant and overstepped God's decrees.
options.note: Verse 5 names this exact charge as the root cause.

options.text: A specific king failed to pay tribute to Assyria.
options.note: Not the stated reason; the charge is a broken covenant with God, not political tribute.

options.text: A famine caused by poor harvests.
options.note: Agricultural collapse is described as a result, verses 7 to 9, not the root cause given in verse 5.

options.text: A border dispute between neighboring cities.
options.note: Not addressed in this passage; the stated cause is covenant-breaking, a moral and spiritual offense.

quiz.q: What surprising element appears in verses 14 to 16 amid the devastation?

options.text: Voices from every direction singing praise, glory to the Righteous One.
options.note: Verses 14 to 16 describe exactly this outburst of praise amid the judgment.

options.text: A total absence of any human response at all.
options.note: The opposite; there is a vivid, vocal response of praise described.

options.text: A rebellion against the LORD by the survivors.
options.note: Not what is described; the response given is worship, not rebellion.

options.text: A new alliance formed between all the surviving nations.
options.note: Not the content of these verses; the specific detail is praise directed to the LORD, not a political alliance.

quiz.q: How does the chapter conclude, in verse 23?

options.text: The LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem with great glory.
options.note: Verse 23 gives this exact, glorious concluding vision.

options.text: The earth is left permanently empty with no future mentioned.
options.note: The opposite; the chapter ends with a positive vision of the LORD's reign, not emptiness.

options.text: A human king is crowned to rule over the restored earth.
options.note: The reign described is specifically the LORD's own reign, not a human king's.

options.text: The sun and moon are restored to full, undimmed brightness.
options.note: The text says the moon is confounded and the sun ashamed, precisely because the LORD's own glory now outshines them, not that they are restored to normal brightness.

quiz.q: How does the broken everlasting covenant in this chapter connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the new, unbreakable everlasting covenant established in Christ's blood.
options.note: Hebrews 13:20 names this new covenant as everlasting and secured in Christ, the answer to the broken covenant here.

options.text: It shows that God abandoned the idea of covenant altogether after this point.
options.note: The opposite; Scripture continues and ultimately fulfills covenant language through Christ.

options.text: It refers only to a covenant between two ancient Near Eastern kings.
options.note: The phrase everlasting covenant elsewhere describes God's covenants with Noah and Abraham, not a purely political treaty.

options.text: It has no connection to any later biblical covenant themes.
options.note: There is a clear canonical link to God's covenant language developed further and ultimately fulfilled in Christ.

questions: This judgment falls on every social class without exception, priest and people, master and servant alike. Are there ways you assume your particular status or role would exempt you from accountability before God?
The chapter names breaking the everlasting covenant as the root cause of the earth's devastation. What covenant commitments, to God or to others, have you been tempted to treat lightly?
Even amid overwhelming devastation, voices rise from every direction singing glory to the Righteous One. Where in your own hard circumstances could you choose to voice praise rather than only lament?

The chapter ends with the LORD reigning gloriously on Mount Zion despite the earth's rebellion. How does the certainty of God's ultimate, visible reign change the way you face uncertainty or chaos in the world today?
Humanity broke God's everlasting covenant, but Christ established a new one that can never be broken. How secure do you feel in that new covenant compared to how you feel about your own faithfulness?

translationNotes.note: The city of chaos likely functions as a representative or symbolic city rather than one specific, named location, standing for human civilization's proud strongholds generally.
Before His elders likely refers to the heavenly council or the elders of Israel witnessing the LORD's glory, an image echoed later in Revelation's twenty four elders around God's throne.
